contest: Americans Against Gun Violence National High School Essay Contest 2020

criteria.name: answers_prompt
criteria.reason: The essay takes a clear position early ("They are completely correct.") and backs regulation in general. The handgun and assault-weapon bans it endorses are only asserted in the last paragraph and never argued for on their own.

criteria.name: specificity
criteria.reason: It has real checkable anchors: the 2019 mass-shooting count, "Nearly 40,000" deaths a year, and District of Columbia v. Heller in 2008. But the cross-state and international claims never name a state, a country or a figure, and lean on footnote numbers like "(5, 6)" and "(7)" instead.

criteria.name: human_voice
criteria.reason: There is a real voice, and some clumsy human moments ("Twice has the Supreme Court ruled", "commonsensical yet apparently evasive"). It is buried under stump-speech tells: balanced antitheses ("sympathy instead of safety"), slogans ("Enough is enough. It's time to fight back."), runs of rhetorical questions, and a punchline at the end of every paragraph ("It's about time we joined them.", "This has to stop.").

criteria.name: stories
criteria.reason: 0 personal stories, which is fine for an analytic prompt. The only case study, Heller, gets a two-sentence summary plus name-calling ("rivaling Dred Scott", "Madison... rolling in his grave") instead of an actual walk through the case.

criteria.name: ideas_mechanism
criteria.reason: The core argument is "Logic dictates that providing a legal incentive against gun ownership will reduce rates" plus a correlation. It never explains how a ban reduces injuries, or why existing laws fail. The only policy is "laws comparable to... other advanced democratic countries", without naming one.

criteria.name: structure_ending
criteria.reason: The paragraph order works: problem, then evidence, then constitutional cause, then a call to act. The close brings back the opening's "thoughts and prayers", but the last line, "I hope you'll join me.", is a stock rally ending.

fixes: Cut at least 53 words to get under the 500 limit (worth +10). Start with the slogan and rhetorical-question lines: "This isn't the American way. Enough is enough. It's time to fight back."; "Why is America so far behind? If the other developed nations have had their eyes opened, why not us? Aren't we supposed to be leading the free world?"; "James Madison... is rolling in his grave..."; "This has to stop." Cutting these also lifts the voice score, because they are the main slogan and punchline tells.

In paragraph 2, replace "Logic dictates..." and the unnamed comparisons with the actual numbers from his own sources (5), (6) and (7): which states, which countries, what rates. Then add one sentence on how a handgun or assault-weapon ban actually lowers injuries, such as fewer guns in homes or fewer high-capacity weapons. Ask Enes which source he trusts for each figure rather than adding new ones. This raises specificity and mechanism.

Rework paragraph 3 into a short, accurate case study. Name the two earlier rulings that "(9, 10)" points to, quote one line of Heller's holding, and drop "With a fantastical decision rivaling Dred Scott" and "a right which does not exist". As written, a judge who disagrees will read these as overclaims, and a judge who agrees gets no evidence from them.
